extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 18th-century fiction; writers/interested readers studying digressive/experimental narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and self-reflections on beginning a book and on the deliberate use of digressions/non‑linear, conversational narrative in a novel. Focuses on starting sentence-by-sentence, seizing fleeting ideas, and when to be careful about sequencing in an intricate tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Way of beginning a book
rubrics_metrics.description: "That of all the several ways of beginning a book which are now in practice throughout the known world, I am confident my own way of doing it is the best... I begin with writing the first sentence—and trusting to Almighty God for the second."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial prescription: start by writing the first sentence and rely on inspiration/providence for what follows rather than overplanning. Sternian justification: this method will 'cure an author for ever of the fuss and folly of opening his street-door ... only to observe how one sentence of mine follows another, and how the plan follows the whole.' (Advice against over‑ceremonial or over‑public planning; favor sentence‑level initiation and momentum.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of digressions and non‑linear structure
rubrics_metrics.description: "I defy the best cabbage planter that ever existed, whether he plants backwards or forwards, it makes little difference in the account ... I defy him to go on coolly, critically, and canonically, planting his cabbages one by one, in straight lines, and stoical distances, especially if slits in petticoats are unsew'd up—without ever and anon straddling out, or sidling into some bastardly digression."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stylistic criterion: embrace digressions and parenthetical excursions as a natural, even necessary, feature of lively/romantic/fanciful narrative. Sterne frames digression as appropriate to a 'clear climate of fantasy' where ideas must vent; straight, strictly linear plotting is presented as an anti‑pattern except in deadened contexts ('Freeze‑land, Fog‑land'). (Implication for writers: allow the narrative to swerve, take conversational turns, and follow associative impulses.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture fleeting ideas promptly
rubrics_metrics.description: "I wish you saw me half starting out of my chair, with what confidence, as I grasp the elbow of it, I look up——catching the idea, even sometimes before it half way reaches me——I believe in my conscience I intercept many a thought which heaven intended for another man."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process recommendation: seize ideas immediately when they occur—physically and mentally interrupt other motions to record or follow them. The passage portrays impatience and energetic interception of thoughts as part of the writer's craft (supports the earlier 'write the first sentence and trust for the next' approach).

rubrics_metrics.name: Be careful with sequencing in an intricate story
rubrics_metrics.description: "—But for heaven’s sake, let us not talk of quarts or gallons——let us take the story straight before us; it is so nice and intricate a one, it will scarce bear the transposition of a single tittle; and, somehow or other, you have got me thrust almost into the middle of it— I beg we may take more care."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial caution: when a narrative is 'nice and intricate' the author warns against careless rearrangement or mishandling—small transpositions can damage coherence. This is a counterpoint to permissive digression: although digressions are pleasurable, the core intricate plot still requires careful handling and attention to sequence and continuity.
